title: Parents as shepherds
hookLine: each of you is a shepherd, and each of you will be asked about the flock

cards: Count the people you'd have to answer for. At dusk, a shepherd does exactly that: one, two, three, all the way through the flock, because if one is missing, the whole evening changes.

A report in Sahih al-Bukhari says the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, once tended sheep himself, for the people of Makkah. So when he described responsibility, he reached for a picture he knew from the inside.
Not a king, not a judge. A shepherd, who walks behind the flock all day and at the end of it has to answer for every one.

teach.h: EACH OF YOU IS A SHEPHERD.
teach.b: The hadith is kept in al-Bukhari, from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar. In paraphrase: each of you is a shepherd, and each of you is responsible for his flock. Then it goes down a list.
The ruler is a shepherd over his people. A man is a shepherd over his household. A woman is a shepherd over her husband's house and his children.
A servant is a shepherd over his master's property. And it ends where it began: each of you is a shepherd, and each of you is responsible for his flock.
The Arabic word is ra'i, the one who tends, and the flock is ra'iyyah, those who are tended. Notice what that word doesn't say. A shepherd doesn't own the sheep in this picture.
The shepherd is trusted with them, and will be asked. Some readers hear in that the difference between possession and trust. A child, in this frame, isn't a project or a trophy.
A child is a flock you were handed, and the question at the end isn't how impressive they turned out. It's how you tended them. And look at who's on the list.
Mother and father both. The ruler, and the servant too.
Nobody is only a sheep; even the least powerful person in the hadith has something in their care.
The Qur'an puts the same weight on the home in surah al-Tahrim, telling believers, in paraphrase, to guard themselves and their families from the Fire.
Tending begins at home, and a shepherd's main tool, every day, is simply being there.

how: Muslims often cite the hadith that each person is a shepherd responsible for their flock when speaking about parents' duties, describing children as a trust rather than a possession.

o: parents as owners who decide everything for their children
a title for leaders of a congregation, not for parents
each person trusted with others in their care, and asked about them

p: over her husband's house and children

s: in the hadith, only rulers are called shepherds
it ends: each of you is a shepherd, responsible for his flock.
a report in al-Bukhari says the Prophet tended sheep himself
in the picture, the shepherd owns the flock
the shepherd is trusted with them, and will be asked about them.

games.q: you're a servant in the hadith's list, with no power over anyone. are you a shepherd?
o: no, only rulers and parents are.
games.why: the hadith names the servant too: a shepherd over his master's property. nobody is only a sheep.

practice: Think of a child in your life, your own, a niece or nephew, a student, or anyone in your care, and picture what they're into right now and what they keep trying to tell you.
See yourself giving them ten unhurried minutes: no phone, no correcting, just attention. If you pray, hold them in your prayer for a moment.

wordCard.voice: Parents as shepherds. In the hadith, everyone is a shepherd over someone, trusted with them, and asked about them. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: shepherd, the one who tends; the flock is ra'iyyah.

carryVoice: Your line: each a shepherd. Trusted, not owning, and asked at the end of the day. Same time tomorrow.
